阅读说明：卫星篇保留 2016 年的历史视角。3 厘米 FemtoSat 的估计发射费不代表标准 CubeSat 总费用；NASA 发射项目有申请和遴选条件，开放设计也不是绝对安全保证。
The future of personal satellite technology is here —are we ready for it?
[A] Satellites used to be the exclusive playthings of rich governments and wealthy corporations. But increasingly, as space becomes more democratized, they are coming within reach of ordinary people. Just like drones (无人机) before them, miniature satellites are beginning to fundamentally transform our conceptions of who gets to do what up above our heads.
[B] As a 2016 report from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine highlights, these satellites hold tremendous potential for making satellite-based science more accessible than ever before. However, as the cost of getting your own satellite in orbit drops sharply, the risks of irresponsible use grow. The question here is no longer “Can we?” but “Should we?” What are the potential downsides of having a slice of space densely populated by equipment built by people not traditionally labeled as “professionals”? And what would the responsible and beneficial development and use of this technology actually look like? Some of the answers may come from a nonprofit organization that has been building and launching amateur satellites for nearly 50 years.
[C] Having your personal satellite launched into orbit might sound like an idea straight out of science fiction. But over the past few decades a unique class of satellites has been created that fits the bill: CubeSats. The “Cube” here simply refers to the satellite's shape. A basic CubeSat unit, called 1U, is approximately 10 cm on each side, so small that a single CubeSat could easily be mistaken for a paperweight on your desk. These mini-satellites can fit in a launch vehicle's formerly “wasted space.” Multiples can be deployed in combination for more complex missions than could be achieved by one CubeSat alone.
[D] Within their compact bodies these minute satellites are able to house sensors and communications receivers/transmitters that enable operators to study Earth from space, as well as space around Earth. Many early CubeSats were designed for Low Earth Orbit (LEO), generally below 2,000 km above Earth. The Hubble Space Telescope and the International Space Station (ISS) also operate in LEO. CubeSats can travel farther; by 2016, NASA was developing CubeSat missions for destinations beyond Earth orbit.
[E] Because they're so small and light, it costs much less to get a CubeSat into Earth's orbit than a traditional communications or GPS satellite. In related work, in April 2016 a research group at Arizona State University estimated that its experimental SunCube FemtoSat, just 3 cm on each side, could cost as little as $3,000 to launch into low Earth orbit. This was a projected launch cost for an especially small spacecraft, not the total cost of a standard CubeSat mission. This decrease in cost allows researchers, hobbyists and even elementary school groups to put simple instruments into LEO or even have them deployed from the ISS.
[F] The CubeSat concept was developed in 1999 by Jordi Puig-Suari at California Polytechnic State University and Bob Twiggs at Stanford University to enable students to design, build, test and operate small spacecraft. NASA and other organizations subsequently adopted the format. Through its CubeSat Launch Initiative and associated Educational Launch of Nanosatellites missions, NASA offered rideshare launch opportunities for selected educational and research projects, including eligible U.S. nonprofits. Participants had to fund spacecraft development, and selection did not guarantee a launch. Clearly, satellites were no longer just for professional aerospace organizations.
[G] The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine report emphasizes CubeSats' importance in scientific discovery and the training of future space scientists and engineers. Yet it also acknowledges that widespread deployment of LEO CubeSats isn't risk-free. The greatest concern the authors raise is space debris - pieces of “junk” that orbit the earth, with the potential to cause serious damage if they collide with operational units, including the ISS.
[H] The 2016 report warned that a growing CubeSat population required attention to tracking and debris mitigation. Yet as LEO opens up to more amateur satellites, they may pose an increasing threat. As the report authors point out, even near-misses might lead to a more burdensome regulatory framework that could affect future science CubeSats.
[I] CubeSat researchers suggest that now's the time to ponder unexpected and unintended possible consequences of more people than ever having access to their own small slice of space. In an era when you can simply buy a CubeSat kit off the shelf, how can we trust the satellites over our heads were developed with good intentions by people who knew what they were doing? Some “expert amateurs” in the satellite game could provide some inspiration for how to proceed responsibly.
[J] In 1969, the Radio Amateur Satellite Corporation (AMSAT) was created in order to foster ham radio enthusiasts' (业余无线电爱好者) participation in space research and communication. It continued the efforts, begun in 1961, by Project OSCAR- a U.S.-based group that built and launched the very first nongovernmental satellite just four years after Sputnik. As an organization of volunteers, AMSAT was putting “amateur” satellites in orbit decades before the current CubeSat craze. And over time, its members have learned a thing or two about responsibility. Here, open-source development has been a central principle. Within the organization, AMSAT has a philosophy of open sourcing everything—making technical data on all aspects of their satellites fully available to everyone in the organization, and when possible, the public. According to a member of the team responsible for FOX 1-A, AMSAT's first CubeSat, sharing designs and implementation details makes unauthorized payloads much harder to conceal. This is an argument for transparency, not a guarantee that abuse is impossible.
[K] However, they're more cautious about sharing information with nonmembers, as the organization guards against others developing the ability to hijack and take control of their satellites. This form of “self-governance” is possible within long-standing amateur organizations that, over time, are able to build a sense of responsibility to community members, as well as society in general. But what happens when new players emerge, who don't have deep roots within the existing culture?
[L] Hobbyists and students are gaining access to technologies without being part of a long-standing amateur establishment. They're still constrained by funders, launch providers and a series of regulations - all of which rein in what CubeSat developers can and cannot do. But there's a danger they're ill-equipped to think through potential unintended consequences. What these unintended consequences might be is admittedly far from clear. Yet we know innovators can be remarkably creative with taking technologies in unexpected directions. Think of something as seemingly benign as the cellphone - we have microfinance and text-based social networking at one end of the spectrum, and improvised (临时制作的) explosive devices at the other.
[M] This is where a culture of social responsibility around CubeSats becomes important - not simply to ensure that physical risks are minimized, but to engage with a much larger community in anticipating and managing less obvious consequences of the technology. This is not an easy task. Yet the evidence from AMSAT and other areas of technology development suggests that responsible amateur communities can and do emerge around novel technologies. The challenge here, of course, is ensuring that what an amateur community considers to be responsible, actually is. Here's where there needs to be a much wider public conversation that extends beyond government agencies and scientific communities to include students, hobbyists, and anyone who may potentially stand to be affected by the use of CubeSat technology.

Questions 46 to 50 are based on the following passage.
阅读说明：职场篇结合个人感受与 2017 年文献综述。低情感投入不等于关系毫无价值；可能的益处和有待研究的机制不宜写成普遍因果结论。
When I re-entered the full-time workforce a few years ago after a decade of solitary self-employment, there was one thing I was looking forward to the most: the opportunity to have work friends once again. It wasn’t until I entered the corporate world that I realized, for me at least, being friends with colleagues didn’t emerge as a priority at all. This is surprising when you consider the prevailing emphasis by scholars and trainers and managers on the importance of cultivating close interpersonal relationships at work. So much research has explored the way in which collegial (同事的) ties can help overcome a range of workplace issues affecting productivity and the quality of work output such as team-based conflict, jealousy, undermining, anger, and more.
Perhaps my expectations of lunches, water-cooler gossip and caring, deep-and-meaningful conversations were a legacy of the last time I was in that kind of office environment. Whereas now, as I near the end of my fourth decade, I realize work can be fully functional and entirely fulfilling without needing to be best mates with the people sitting next to you.
In a review published in 2017 in the Journal of Management, researchers have looked at the concept of “indifferent relationships”. The term encapsulates (概括) relationships with little emotional investment: they can be non-intimate and replaceable, yet still serve useful functions at work.
Indifferent relationships involve little positive or negative feeling. The review discussed limited evidence suggesting that emotional distance, avoidance of conflict and a lack of shared interests can contribute to them. Relationships may also fade when people do not invest effort in maintaining them. I think of this last tendency as being socially lazy: maintaining relationships over the long term takes effort. For some of us, too much effort.
As noted above, indifferent relationships may not always be the most helpful approach in resolving some of the issues that pop up at work. But the review discusses several potential benefits. One is efficiency: spending less effort maintaining a relationship may leave more time for work and productive output (产出). These benefits depend on circumstances.
Another possibility concerns self-esteem. People sometimes make downward comparisons with acquaintances more readily than with close friends. The review suggests that this may support a sense of self-worth, while identifying it as an area for further research. It does not show that everyone benefits by looking down on colleagues.
Ego aside, the review also suggests that emotional neutrality may make critical evaluation easier, while weak ties can connect people with new information. These are possible functions of such relationships, not proof that close friendships are generally unhelpful. None of that might be as fun as after-work socializing but, hey, I’ll take it anyway.

A) Making new friends with his workmates was not as easy as he had anticipated.
B) Cultivating positive interpersonal relationships helped him expel solitary feelings.

D) Building close relationships with his colleagues was not as important as he had expected.
47. What do we learn from many studies about collegial relationships?
A) Inharmonious relationships have an adverse effect on productivity.
B) Harmonious relationships are what many companies aim to cultivate.
C) Close collegial relationships contribute very little to product quality.
D) Conflicting relationships in the workplace exist almost everywhere.
48. What does the review suggest about indifferent workplace relationships?
A) They should be cultivated.
B) They can serve useful functions without emotional closeness.
C) They are vital to corporate culture.
D) They should be reasonably intimate.
49. What does the author say about people who are socially lazy?
A) They feel uncomfortable when engaging in social interactions.
B) They often find themselves in confrontation with their colleagues.
C) They are unwilling to make efforts to maintain workplace relationships.
D) They lack basic communication skills in dealing with interpersonal issues.
50. Which potential benefit of indifferent relationships does the author discuss?
A) They provide fun at work.
B) They help control emotions.
C) They help resolve differences.
D) They may leave more time and effort for work.
Passage Two
Questions 51 to 55 are based on the following passage.
阅读说明：AI 篇为 2017 年前后的观点文章，不是当前技术能力报告。按 Waymo 原始统计修正接管率降幅与平均里程；未来能力和教育建议属于作者判断。
I expect that in the coming decades artificial intelligence (AI) may surpass many of the abilities that we believe make us special. This is a grand challenge for our age and it may require an “irrational” response.
One of the most significant pieces of news from the US in early 2017 was the efforts of Google to make autonomous driving a reality. In its report released in early 2017, Waymo, formerly Google’s self-driving car project, recorded 635,868 miles (about 1,023,330 km) of autonomous driving in California during the 2016 reporting period, with 124 reportable disengagements. That is about one per 5,128 miles, or 8,253 km. Its rounded rate fell from 0.8 per thousand miles in 2015 to 0.2 in 2016, a 75% reduction. The rapid year-to-year decline especially impressed me, though a lower disengagement rate by itself does not establish that a vehicle is safer than a human driver in every setting.
Driving once seemed to be a very human skill. But we said that about chess, too. Then a computer beat the human world champion, repeatedly. Go (围棋) was another long-standing challenge for artificial intelligence. In March 2016, AlphaGo defeated leading professional Lee Sedol by four games to one. With computers conquering what used to be deeply human tasks, what will it mean in the future to be human? I worry about my six-year-old son. What will his place be in a world where machines beat us in one area after another? I wonder which skills will still give him an advantage as machines improve. Actually, it all comes down to a fairly simple question: What’s so special about us? It can’t be skills like arithmetic, which machines already excel in. In this 2017 perspective, I see open-ended human creativity as especially difficult for machines to reproduce: it can go beyond predictable routines without being mere randomness.
Perhaps, if we continue to improve information-processing machines, we’ll soon have helpful rational assistants. So we must aim to complement the rationality of the machine, rather than to compete with it. If I'm right, we should foster a creative spirit because a dose of illogical creativity will complement the rationality of the machine. Unfortunately, however, our education system has not caught up to the approaching reality. I worry that schools and universities put too much emphasis on routine reasoning and skills tied to older machines. We should still teach fact-based reasoning while also encouraging original ideas. We need to help our children learn how to best work with smart computers to improve human decision-making. But most of all we need to keep the long-term perspective in mind: that even if computers will outsmart us, we can still be the most creative. Because if we aren’t, we won’t be providing much value in future ecosystems, and that may put in question the foundation for our existence.
51. What is the author’s greatest concern about the use of AI?
A) Computers are performing lots of creative tasks.
B) Many abilities will cease to be unique to human beings.
C) Computers may become more rational than humans.
D) Many human skills are fast becoming outdated.
52. What aspect of the reported driving data especially impressed the author?
A) Google’s experimental driverless cars require little human intervention.
B) Google’s cars have surpassed his driving ability in just a single year.
C) Waymo reported a rapid reduction in disengagements per mile.
D) Google has become a world leader in the field of autonomous driving.
53. How does the author view human creativity in this 2017 essay?
A) It is rational.
B) It is predictable.
C) It is human specific.
D) Its open-ended forms are difficult for machines to reproduce.
54. What should schools help children do in the era of AI?
A) Cultivate original thinking.
B) Learn to work independently.
C) Compete with smart machines.
D) Understand how AI works.
55. According to the author, how can people continue to contribute value in a future with smarter machines?
A) By constantly outsmarting computers.
B) By adopting a long-term perspective.
C) By rationally compromising with AI.
D) By providing value with our creativity.

Directions: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to translate a passage from Chinese into English. You should write your answer on Answer Sheet 2.
翻译说明：以 2018 年前后的汉语传播为背景，区分语言和书写系统；共同书面语能帮助交流，但不保证消除所有方言理解障碍。
汉语是世界上母语使用者众多的语言之一。汉语的书写系统与许多使用字母的语言不同，主要使用汉字(character)记录语言。汉字有三千多年的历史，是沿用至今的古老书写系统之一。在中国，来自不同地区的人可能听不懂对方的方言，但共同的书面语有助于跨方言交流；这并不意味着所有人都不存在理解困难。汉语历史上对团结中华民族发挥了重要作用。在 2018 年前后，随着中国经济的快速增长和全球影响力的增强，越来越多其他国家的人也开始学习汉语。
